title: Speaking for the women
hook: he asks the Buddha whether women can awaken, and the answer is yes (Vinaya, Cullavagga 10)

segments.voice: Yesterday: twenty-five years of Ananda's quiet service, and your line, like a shadow that never leaves. Today the attendant does something louder.

Early on this path, we stood outside a hall at Vesali with Mahapajapati and the women who had walked there, dusty and in tears, to ask to be ordained. We heard Ananda go in for them. Today we stay with Ananda: the exact question he asked, what came back, and what it cost him much later. The Vinaya, the monks' own rulebook, keeps all three. A request has been turned down three times. Ananda decides not to ask the same thing a fourth time. He asks something else.
screen: `BACK AT VESALI.` → `NO, THREE TIMES.` → `HE ASKS SOMETHING ELSE.`

segments.voice: First, the question. Ananda stops asking whether women may go forth, and asks whether they can. In paraphrase: Lord, if a woman goes forth into the homeless life, is she able to realize the fruits of the path, even full awakening? It's a question about ability, not permission. Second, the answer. Yes, Ananda. They are able. That yes is written into the Vinaya itself. Then Ananda speaks for one woman in particular. Mahapajapati, he reminds the Buddha, was the Buddha's own aunt and foster mother, who nursed him and fed him after his mother died. And the Buddha agrees to ordain women, with eight special rules. Third, the garland. Ananda carries the rules out to Mahapajapati, and she answers with a picture, in paraphrase: as a young person who has just bathed would take a garland of flowers in both hands and set it on their own head, so I take these rules. Buddhists today read that moment in different ways. Some hear grace in her acceptance. Others question the rules themselves and their history. Both readings are part of the conversation now. Fourth, the cost. After the Buddha's death, at a gathering of elders, Ananda is charged with faults, and one of them is that he worked to have women ordained. His answer, in paraphrase: I did it because Mahapajapati had nursed the Blessed One. I don't see it as a fault. But out of respect for you, I confess it. He confessed, and didn't pretend he had changed his mind. Speaking up for someone can be counted against you long after. The text keeps that too.
screen: `MAY THEY, OR CAN THEY?` · `YES, ANANDA. THEY ARE ABLE.` · `A GARLAND ON HER HEAD.` · `COUNTED AGAINST HIM, LATER.` · then, large: `WOMEN CAN AWAKEN.`

segments.voice: Think of a room where things get decided, at work, in your family, in a group you belong to, and one person who isn't heard there. Silently shape one plain question, like Ananda's, that asks what's true about them rather than what's allowed, and rest with the breath, noticing how it sits.
Mahapajapati. The Buddha's aunt and foster mother, for whom Ananda pleaded, the first woman ordained, who took the eight special rules like a garland.
Your line: women can awaken. The answer was yes, and the Vinaya kept it. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Buddhist tradition Mahapajapati is remembered as the first nun, and Ananda as the one who spoke up for the women.

original.note: Pali: arahantship, full awakening; what Ananda asked whether women could realize.

trapdoor: what you thought: Ananda talked the Buddha into letting women join.
what it means: he changed the question from may they to can they, and the answer was yes: women are able to awaken.
what a scholar hears: the yes stands in the Vinaya's chapter on the nuns, and the same Vinaya later records the elders counting Ananda's advocacy as a fault.

chat.says: Did the Buddha say women could reach awakening?
options: Yes. Asked if women who go forth are able to awaken, he said they are able.
He never answered; Ananda decided the question on his own.
Only women of royal birth, like his aunt, were said to be able.
chat.meaning: In the Vinaya, Ananda asks whether a woman who goes forth can realize full awakening, and the Buddha answers: yes, they are able.

Vesali.meaning: a city where the women came to ask to be ordained

Mahapajapati.meaning: the Buddha's aunt and foster mother, the first woman ordained

Blessed One.meaning: a respectful title for the Buddha

notes: All Vinaya material paraphrased (Rhys Davids and Oldenberg, SBE 20, could be quoted if verified).

Year one, day 70 told the walk to Vesali, the three refusals and the 'are they able' turn; this day recaps briefly and adds the garland image and the council charge. Confirm the overlap is acceptable.
Confirm Cullavagga 10.1.4: Mahapajapati's garland simile (a young person, fond of ornaments, freshly bathed, receiving a garland of lotus or jasmine and placing it on the head).

Confirm Cullavagga 11.1.10: among the faults charged to Ananda, his effort for women's going forth; his reply that Mahapajapati had nursed the Buddha, that he saw no fault, but confessed out of faith in the elders.
The eight garudhammas are named but not listed; their interpretation is contested today, and the script says so without taking sides.
